There is this famous textbook about probability, I forget the name. On the inside cover the author puts a giant, boldfaced, statement of the fundamental truth about probability, and therefore statistics too. It says, "There is no such thing as probability," or something very similar. All you can do is come up with a system that is consistent and seems correct to whomever devised it, and hopefully his audience, but there is no scientific way to calculate REAL probabilities in an open system such as this world we all live in. In mundane cases of things that happen frequently this isn't a big deal, but in extraordinary cases, such as tails of a hand-wavingly assembled probability distribution, there should be no expectation that the calculated probability reflects the real probability.

One might ask, "How about those physics experiments where they say there should be one ultra-high energy cosmic rays every five years," or something. They are able to make those calculations because they normalize their statistics against real data. There is no realistic chance that one could find the correct probabilistic tail behavior purely through the application of the theory of statistics. So then when it extends to to even more unlikely things than that which can at least be measured, a reasonable person can have no confidence in the agreement of a purely theoretical statistical distribution's tails with the actual tail behavior observed in nature. If one considers the main body of the distribution, it can probably trusted if it was derived by a well-trained statistician, but only a fucking schmuck would extend that reasoning to the tail behavior.

I bring this up because often times the purpose of calculating statistical distributions is to cause a group to come to agreement on the likelihood of of a very unlikely event occurring, which would be the untrusted tail part rather than the ordinary central part. For instance, you might derive something that says the probability of something is one-in-a-googolplex, and thereby convince everyone it will never happen, when the real frequency might be more like one-in-a-million, which is almost guaranteed to happen... depending on the sample rate and the maximum duration of the window in which happening or not-happening will occur.

PS: And even after normalizing against real data, cosmic rays are interesting because they still, even now in 2017, occur at a rate much higher than the probability distribution says they should. For normal energy rays only, the probability distribution is in good agreement with the real cosmic flux.

PPS: Statistics can appear consistent when you only check them against ordinary cases. How could you check against tail cases? Tail cases don't happen often enough to be available for random data sampling. However, even without being a scientist, everyone should know that the history of the world is summed up by one long string of tail cases. Then when any reasonable person asks themselves, "Can I use statistics to predict future arc of history?," the answer is absolutely no. A fool might answer, "Kinda," but the true answer is no.

PPPS: None of this should be new to anyone with even intermediate training in mathematics.
